passages.t: A God who is near, and the day at Horeb
passages.happening:
Moses turns from the story to its lesson. “Hear now, O Israel, the statutes and ordinances I am teaching you to follow, so that you may live” (verse 1). Nothing is to be added to God's commands and nothing taken away (verse 2). The people have just seen what happened at Baal-peor, where those who followed another god died, ‘but you who held fast to the LORD your God are alive to this day’ (verse 4).

Keeping these laws will show Israel's wisdom to the nations (verse 6). Moses asks two questions. “For what nation is great enough to have a god as near to them as the LORD our God is to us whenever we call on Him? And what nation is great enough to have righteous statutes and ordinances like this entire law I set before you today?” (verses 7-8).

Then he takes them back to the mountain. It blazed with fire, wrapped in cloud and darkness. “And the LORD spoke to you out of the fire. You heard the sound of the words, but saw no form; there was only a voice” (verse 12). God declared his covenant, the Ten Commandments, and wrote them on two tablets of stone (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The first word, ‘Hear’, is the word that will open the great confession of chapter 6. In Hebrew, to hear is also to heed.

Baal-peor was fresh in every mind. It had happened in the valley where they were now camped (3:29). Israelite men had joined in the worship of a local god, and a plague followed. Numbers 25 tells the story. Moses starts his sermon on idols with the bodies they had just buried.

Verses 6 to 8 would have surprised a people who had nothing. They had no city, no temple and no king. Moses tells them what they do have. They have a God who is near when they call, and they have laws that are just. Other nations will look at how Israel lives and call it wise. The law is not a burden hidden away. It is meant to be seen.

The command to guard the memory is urgent. ‘Do not forget the things your eyes have seen.’ Most of those listening had been children at Horeb, or were not yet born. Moses still says ‘you stood’ and ‘you heard’. The memory belongs to the whole people, and each generation must hand it to the next: “Teach them to your children and grandchildren” (verse 9).

The center of the passage is what Israel did not see. There was fire, cloud and a voice. There was no shape. The Hebrew word for ‘form’ comes five times in this chapter, and the whole argument hangs on it. Moses will draw the conclusion in the next passage.
passages.later:
Numbers tells what happened at Peor: “So Israel joined in worshiping Baal of Peor, and the anger of the LORD burned against them” (Numbers 25:3).

King Solomon, praying at the temple, echoed Moses' wonder: “O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like You in heaven above or on earth below” (1 Kings 8:23).

John's Gospel begins from the same fact, that God has not been seen, and says what has happened since: “No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known” (John 1:18).
passages.asks: Moses tells a people with no city and no king that they are rich: God is near when they call. Ask whether you count that as wealth. And think of verse 9. Ask what your eyes have seen of God's goodness that could slip from your heart if you do not tell it to someone younger.

passages.t: No image; a jealous God and a merciful God
passages.happening:
Moses draws the rule from the memory. “So since you saw no form of any kind on the day the LORD spoke to you out of the fire at Horeb, be careful that you do not act corruptly and make an idol for yourselves of any form or shape” (verses 15-16). No likeness of man or woman, animal, bird, creeping thing or fish. And when they look up at the sun, moon and stars, they are not to bow down to them (verse 19).

God took Israel ‘out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt’ to be his own (verse 20). Moses repeats that he himself will die east of the Jordan (verses 21-22). Then the warning: “For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God” (verse 24).

He looks far ahead. If, after many years in the land, Israel makes idols, ‘you will quickly perish from the land’ (verse 26). God will scatter them among the peoples, and there they will serve gods of wood and stone (verses 27-28).

“But if from there you will seek the LORD your God, you will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul” (verse 29). “For the LORD your God is a merciful God; He will not abandon you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
In the world around Israel, a god's statue was far more than a reminder. In Mesopotamia a newly made image went through a ritual of washing and of opening its mouth. After that it was treated as the god's living presence. Priests clothed it, set meals before it, and carried it in procession.

That is what stands behind verse 28, with its gods ‘which cannot see or hear or eat or smell’. And it is why Moses' rule was so strange in its world. Israel's God would not be housed in an object. The point is not that God has a shape he chose to hide. It is that nothing made, in the sky or on the earth or in the water, can stand for him.

The warning about the sun, moon and stars was not idle. The books of Kings report that in later centuries kings of Judah built altars to the host of heaven, and that King Josiah removed the priests who burned incense to them.

‘Jealous’ can sound ugly in English. The Hebrew word is used in the Bible only of God. It is not petty envy. It is the rightful, exclusive love of a husband for his wife. God has bound himself to this people, and he will not share them with a block of wood.

Treaties between kings in the ancient world called on the gods of both sides as witnesses. Israel may name no other god, so Moses calls ‘heaven and earth’ (verse 26).

Then comes the turn that makes this chapter precious. The same God who is a consuming fire in verse 24 is a merciful God in verse 31. The scattering is not the end. ‘From there’, from the far country and the worst of their failure, they may seek him and find him. The word for ‘return’ in verse 30 is the Old Testament's main word for repentance. It means turning around, and it means coming home.

Readers date this passage in different ways. The northern kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC, and Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC. Scholars who date much of Deuteronomy late often see these verses as written for people who had already lost the land. Readers who hold that the words come from Moses take them as a covenant warning given beforehand, as ancient treaties gave. On either view the promise is the same.
passages.later:
The second of the Ten Commandments is the rule Moses preaches here: “You shall not make for yourself an idol in the form of anything in the heavens above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath” (Exodus 20:4).

Psalm 115 mocks the idols in Moses' words: ‘They have mouths, but cannot speak; they have eyes, but cannot see’ (Psalm 115:5).

Jeremiah wrote to the exiles in Babylon with the promise of verse 29: “You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart” (Jeremiah 29:13).

The letter to the Hebrews quotes verse 24 to Christians: ‘For our God is a consuming fire’ (Hebrews 12:29).

And Paul says of Jesus what could be said of no carved thing: “The Son is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15).
passages.hard:
Verse 19 says the sun, moon and stars are what God ‘has apportioned to all the nations under heaven’. Did God give the other nations the stars as their gods?

Readers have understood the verse in three main ways.

Some take it to mean only that God gave the lights of the sky to all peoples for light and for marking the seasons, as in Genesis 1. They belong to the whole world, so Israel must not worship them.

Others, following an old Jewish and Christian reading, take it to mean that God let the nations go their own way into idolatry for a time, while choosing Israel for himself. Paul says something like it: “In past generations, He let all nations go their own way” (Acts 14:16).

A third view connects the verse with 32:8, where the Berean Standard Bible, following some ancient copies, says that God set the boundaries of the peoples ‘according to the number of the sons of God’. On this reading the host of heaven are created beings set over the nations, to whom the nations wrongly gave worship.

On every reading the chapter is clear about one thing. These are not gods. Moses says that ‘the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth below; there is no other’ (verse 39). The verse describes the world as Israel found it. It does not permit the worship it forbids, and it gives no ground for looking down on any people.
passages.asks: An idol is a god cut down to a size a person can manage. Ask what picture of God you have made for yourself that is easier to live with than the God who spoke from the fire. And if you are far from God today, hear the words ‘from there’. Ask what it would mean to seek him from where you are, and not from where you think you should be.

passages.happening:
Moses tells the people to search all of time and all the world. “Has anything as great as this ever happened or been reported? Has a people ever heard the voice of God speaking out of the fire, as you have, and lived?” (verses 32-33). Has any god ever taken one nation out of another, with signs and wonders, ‘as the LORD your God did for you in Egypt, before your eyes?’ (verse 34).

“You were shown these things so that you would know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides Him” (verse 35).

He gives the reason for it all. “Because He loved your fathers, He chose their descendants after them and brought you out of Egypt by His presence and great power” (verse 37).

So: “Know therefore this day and take to heart that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth below; there is no other” (verse 39). They are to keep his commands, so that it may go well with them and their children in the land (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
The sermon has been climbing toward this. Moses asks questions he knows the answer to. No people had ever heard God speak and lived. No god had ever done what the LORD did in Egypt. Israel's faith rests on things that happened in front of witnesses.

Twice he says, ‘there is no other’. In a world full of gods, each with its own city and its own people, this was a bold claim. Israel's God is not the strongest god among many. He is God in heaven and on earth, and beside him there is none.

Verse 37 is the first time the book says why God did all this. The reason is love. He loved the fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and so he chose their children. Israel did nothing to bring it about. Moses will say this again more than once, so that Israel never mistakes a gift for a wage.

Notice the order of verses 39 and 40. First comes knowing: ‘take to heart that the LORD is God’. Then comes doing: ‘Keep His statutes’. Obedience in Deuteronomy grows out of knowing who God is and what he has done.
passages.later:
The prophet Isaiah heard God say the same words to a people in exile: “I am the LORD, and there is no other; there is no God but Me” (Isaiah 45:5).

A scribe in Jerusalem once answered Jesus with this chapter's confession: “You have stated correctly that God is One and there is no other but Him” (Mark 12:32).
passages.asks: Moses asks Israel to know something and then to take it to heart. Ask what you know about God that has not yet reached the place where you make your choices. And read verse 37 slowly. Ask whether you believe that God's love for you began with him and not with anything you did.

passages.t: Three cities of refuge, and a heading
passages.happening:
The speech ends, and the narrator records an act. “Then Moses set aside three cities across the Jordan to the east to which a manslayer could flee after killing his neighbor unintentionally without prior malice” (verses 41-42). They are Bezer for Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead for Gad, and Golan in Bashan for Manasseh (verse 43).

Then comes a heading for what follows. “This is the law that Moses set before the Israelites” (verse 44). It names the place again: the valley opposite Beth-peor, in the land taken from Sihon and Og (verses 46-49).
passages.hearers:
The three cities lie in the lands just given to the two and a half tribes in chapter 3.

Behind them stands an old custom. When someone was killed, a close relative was expected to take the killer's life in return. A person who had killed someone by accident, as when an axe head flies off its handle and strikes a neighbor (19:5), could flee to one of these towns. There he was protected until his case could be heard. Chapter 19 gives the full law, and so does Numbers 35.

It is worth noticing what Moses does the moment he finishes preaching. He has just said that Israel's laws are more just than any nation's (verse 8). He goes straight from the sermon to setting up a protection for the person most likely to be killed unfairly.

Verses 44 to 49 work like a title page. The first address is over. The second and longest address begins in the next chapter, with the Ten Commandments.
passages.later:
Numbers gives the purpose of these cities: “You are to have these cities as a refuge from the avenger, so that the manslayer will not die until he stands trial before the assembly” (Numbers 35:12).

Joshua later completed the number, adding three cities west of the Jordan, as the book of Joshua records (Joshua 20:7-8).
passages.asks: Moses' first act after his sermon was to protect a person from being punished for what he did not mean to do. Ask whether you leave room, in your judgments of others, for the difference between harm that was intended and harm that was an accident. And ask who near you needs a place of safety while the truth is found out.
